General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Strange fresh materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1216 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most materials simply react when something pushes, pulls, or bends them.
  • In a recent development, everyday materials such as metal, concrete, glass, and rubber are generally considered passive.
  • Industry observers note that active matter works differently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most materials simply react when something pushes, pulls, or bends them. But a very different category of matter can draw on its own energy to change shape and respond to outside forces in surprising ways. Known as active matter, these unusual materials are attracting growing scientific interest. Now, physicists from the universities of Amsterdam, Fresh South Wales, and Cambridge have uncovered remarkable new behaviors that could change how future machines and robots are designed.

In a recent development, everyday materials such as metal, concrete, glass, and rubber are generally considered passive. They can stretch, bend, shift, or change shape when forces act on them, but the energy needed to produce those changes comes from outside the material.

Industry observers note that active matter works differently. It contains an internal source of energy that allows it to respond to its surroundings in ways ordinary materials cannot. Many examples occur naturally in living systems. A flock of birds, for instance, can move together as a coordinated group, adjusting its behavior in response to wind, changes in the landscape, available food, or a suitable place to rest.

Recent findings suggest that scientists can also recreate some of these remarkable properties in the laboratory. Researchers from the University of Amsterdam (The Netherlands), the University of Cambridge (UK), and the University of New South Wales (Sydney, Australia) have spent several years developing active materials from surprisingly simple components, including miniature motors, rods, and rubber bands. Their experiments have revealed unusual mechanical behaviors with potentially valuable applications, leading to two recently accepted scientific papers.

Scientists Create Materials That Can Crawl, Walk, and Dig.

One of the discoveries involves two familiar mechanical behaviors known as buckling and snapping.

Recent findings suggest that imagine squeezing a paper ticket between your fingers. As the pressure increases, the ticket becomes unstable and bends to one side. If you then press against the curved surface, it initially pushes back before suddenly flipping in the opposite direction.

According to recent reports, this is how ordinary passive materials behave. External forces supply the energy needed for the ticket to buckle and snap, and each action occurs only once in response to the applied force.

Industry observers note that the researchers discovered that adding internal activity can fundamentally transform this behavior. They assembled a series of connected rods into a flexible chain, placing small motors at the joints where neighboring rods meet. These motors created interactions that were not symmetrical. Moving one rod could affect its neighbor in a different way than moving that neighbor would affect the original rod (by rotating over a different angle, for example).

The result was striking. When external forces acted on these active chains, they still bent and snapped, but the movement no longer had to end after a single event. Instead, the structures could repeatedly buckle and snap, producing ongoing oscillations.

In a recent development, the underlying physics involves a transformation of the system's critical point, where snapping normally takes place, into what researchers call a critical exceptional point. This unusual behavior makes it possible for the chains to generate movements resembling crawling, walking, and even digging.

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, with Sami Al-Izzi of the University of New South Wales and Yao Du of the University of Amsterdam serving as joint first authors. One of the team's buckling chains was also featured on the journal's cover.

Industry observers note that beyond revealing unexpected physics, the discovery points toward a promising approach to building materials capable of performing multiple tasks autonomously. Such structures could be especially useful in flexible, "soft" robots, potentially allowing their bodies to produce complex movements without relying on a centralized control system.

Active Matter Challenges a Fundamental Engineering Principle.

A separate investigation by the same international research team uncovered another surprising property of active materials, this time challenging a principle widely used in engineering.

Whether designing large bridges or tiny nanomechanical devices, engineers depend on established rules that connect the properties of individual components to the behavior of an entire structure.

According to recent reports, one such rule is Le Chatelier's Principle. In the mechanical context described by the researchers, it suggests that changes made to individual parts of a system should produce corresponding changes in the overall structure. For example, making a structure's individual components stiffer would generally be expected to increase the stiffness of the entire assembly.

It has been revealed that but the researchers found that active matter does not always follow this expectation. In some cases, increasing the activity of individual components can actually reduce the activity of the material as a whole.

According to recent reports, to investigate this counterintuitive effect, the scientists built another structure using motors and rods. Rather than arranging the components in a chain, they connected them into a flat, two-dimensional network resembling a lattice. They then examined how the elastic behavior of the entire structure changed depending on the properties of its individual elements.

Industry observers note that their experiments revealed that the overall response depended on more than simply how active each component was. What mattered was whether the active elements formed connected pathways capable of transmitting mechanical responses throughout the structure.

Why More Activity Can Produce Less Response.

The researchers identified a process called percolation as the key to understanding this unexpected behavior.

Recent findings suggest that A useful comparison is the movement of water through ground coffee. If the coffee grounds are packed too tightly, water cannot easily travel through the entire layer. The arrangement of the grounds determines whether the water can find a continuous path.

Something similar happens inside active materials. If too many of the interconnected components have relatively low activity, they can prevent elastic responses from spreading through the structure. Even when other components are extremely active, their influence may not extend across the entire material.

This explains why making some parts more active does not necessarily produce a more active structure overall. The way the components are connected and distributed can be just as important as their individual properties.

The second study, led by first author Jack Binysh from Corentin Coulais's research group at the University of Amsterdam, was published in Physical Review X.

The researchers believe that this unexpected departure from Le Chatelier's Principle could have vital implications for understanding and designing systems built from active microscopic structures. These include biological gels, epithelial monolayers, which are sheets of closely connected cells, and neuromorphic networks that mimic aspects of biological information processing.

It has been revealed that together, the findings reveal how dramatically materials can behave when their internal components actively consume energy and interact in unconventional ways. The discoveries could influence research across physics, soft matter science, mechanical engineering, the life sciences, and robotics, while opening latest possibilities for creating adaptable materials and smarter robotic systems.

  • It has been revealed that the Heartopia X My Little Pony event officially begins on February 14, but a pre-launch login event is now live through the actual collaboration’s start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that heartopia has officially shared initial details about its first-ever collaboration event. The game, which launched a month ago to great success on mobile, as well as Steam on PC, has already been a staple among fans of Animal Crossing and The Sims.

Things are kicking into gear, it seems, because the game is already about to host its first collaboration event, and it is with My Little Pony.

It has been revealed that the Heartopia X My Little Pony event officially begins on February 14, but a pre-launch login event is now live through the actual collaboration’s start. The limited-time event offers players sign-in puzzles every day that will unlock time-limited Exhibition Passes.

The first actual piece of My Little Pony-themed content can be yours if you complete all puzzles, as that gets you a limited edition costume for your pet, based on the show’s Spike. The event itself, which will be available until March 15, brings My Little Pony’s Tree of Harmony into the world of Heartopia.

The ponies need your help to Wield Elements of Harmony so they can reawaken the tree, and bring it back to Equestria. In gameplay terms, you’re going to want to perform daily sensing at the tree in order to earn three of the six Elements of Harmony: Honesty, Generosity, Loyalty, Kindness, Laughter, and Magic.

The more you do this, the more the tree’s Energy goes up, and the more rewards and resources you stand to earn. Even more time-limited Exhibition Passes, and Moonlight Crystals can be earned as you water the tree.

Badge Pull Tokens are your massive reward, which is what you’re actually going to use to get the special Pony Series badges. You’ll earn ten time-limited Exhibition Passes each time you complete one of the three sets of Pony Series badges. Collect all three and you’ll earn Town Collaboration Series badges.

According to recent reports, heartopia is a free-to-play game, so you know there is a Gacha component to this event. Expect six non-replacement Gacha Pools that each map to one member of My Little Pony’s Mane Six. Within each pool, you’ll be able to earn five outfit pieces, and one vehicle.

We also recently updated our guides on how to catch Frostspore fish - and if you’re into cooking, how to obtain every recipe and variant. If you haven’t already, definitely see if you missed any of these Heartopia codes, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2026 Acura Integra Type S is officially for sale in Japan. That might not seem like major news, considering Honda Motor Organization is headquartered in Japan, but the release marks the first Acura-branded vehicle to be exported to the Japanese market. While this is Acura’s first time in Japan, it’s strangely not the Integra’s, which spent a few decades wearing a Honda badge from 1985 to 2006.

Most Acuras are designed and built in the United States and sold throughout North America. The latest Integras for sale in Japan are the same as those sold stateside, meaning they’ll be left-hand-drive anomalies in a predominantly right-hand-drive market.

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 50219.

That also means they’ll get the same 320-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four that we’re quite fond of in the United States. The front-wheel-drive sport compact is only offered with a six-speed manual transmission and features a limited-slip differential, Brembo brakes, and 19-inch wheels wrapped in summer tires. The whole package comes together to reach 60 mph in a brisk 5.1 seconds.

According to recent reports, honda builds every Integra Type S at its assembly plant in Marysville, Ohio, and the engines come from Honda’s Anna Engine Plant, also located in Ohio. Honda began exporting vehicles from Ohio to Japan in 1988 and has shipped nearly 300,000 Hondas to Japan since then.

Recent findings suggest that honda says the Teg’s introduction in Japan marks a strong global demand for an enthusiast-centered performance sedan. If the Type S is well-received in the Japanese market, it’s likely that more Acuras could start making their way to Japan in the future. Pricing and the exact number of Integra Type S models available in Japan haven’t been released yet, but considering they’re identical to the Type S models sold on our shores, they’ll likely come in around $56,000.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hacker has pleaded guilty to a number of online crimes, including the 2022 breach of Rockstar Games which resulted in a bunch of mid-development clips of GTA 6 in action leaking onto the net.

The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17. Kurtaj, now aged 21, was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital indefinitely due to the severity of his autism, but was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial. He'll be sentenced at a later date.

It has been revealed that kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes. The Rockstar hack was reportedly done using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel room's TV, plus a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

Sources indicate that 90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 were flung online by that hack, with Rockstar having refused to cooperate with Kurtaj's demand via an internal Slack channel that the tech giant contact him on massaging app Telegram within 24 hours. Rockstar claimed the breach cost them $5m million to recover from, in addition to staff having to waste thousands of hours.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, GTA 6 suffered yet another leak, with a hacker or hackers going by "Cyberleek" posting various videos of the game in action. Rockstar and parent company Take-Two swiftly sprung into action, taking down videos, filing subpoenas, and issuing a statement that called the leak "heartbreaking".

Hopefully with the game's console release later this week, those will be the only two GTA 6 leaks which have to be added to the annals of gaming history. As much as marketing can leave a bad taste in the mouth, especially when it barely indicates anything of the actual product being advertised, neither of the GTA 6 leaks served much of a purpose beyond forcing people to waste some time and energy talking about the perpetrators.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, marking a major setback in the fight against a highly contagious disease.
  • The United States first achieved measles elimination status in 2000.
  • It has been revealed that the announcement comes during the country's worst measles resurgence in decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, marking a major setback in the fight against a highly contagious disease. At the same time, a fresh nationwide survey from the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) reveals that many Americans remain confused about the dangers of measles and the vaccines that protect against it.

The United States first achieved measles elimination status in 2000. This designation meant that no strain of the virus had spread continuously within the country for 12 months or longer. However, on Nov. 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization confirmed that the United States no longer qualified for that status.

It has been revealed that the announcement comes during the country's worst measles resurgence in decades. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the United States had recorded 5,412 confirmed cases in 2026 as of Nov. 12. That is more than twice the 2,290 cases reported throughout all of 2025.

Vaccine Myths Persist Despite Decades of Scientific Evidence.

In a recent development, A November 2026 Annenberg Science and Public Health (ASAPH) survey, conducted using adults from the SSRS Omnibus survey, highlights widespread misunderstandings about childhood vaccination. Nearly two-thirds of Americans (64%) correctly rejected the claim that "vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps, and rubella cause autism." However, 17% believed the claim was true, while another 19% mentioned they did not know whether it was true or false.

Industry observers note that the results closely resemble findings from earlier APPC research. Across four surveys involving a separate sample of U.S. adults (September 2024 to August 2026), the ongoing ASAPH national probability survey found that 65% to 68% correctly rejected a connection between childhood vaccines and autism (65%-68%). Another 12% to 14% incorrectly believed there was a connection (12%-14%), while 19% to 22% remained uncertain.

In a recent development, the latest survey also asked respondents to compare autism rates among fully vaccinated and unvaccinated children. Nearly half (49%) believed both groups were "about as likely" to show signs of autism. Another 11% thought fully vaccinated children were "more likely" to show signs, 14% believed they were "less likely," and 26% could not say.

Extensive scientific research has found no evidence that vaccines cause autism. In 2004, the National Academy of Medicine (then named the Institute of Medicine) concluded that "the body of epidemiological evidence favors rejection of a causal relationship between the MMR vaccine and autism evidence.".

The World Health Organization's Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety reached the same conclusion in 2025, reaffirming that high-quality scientific evidence does not establish a causal relationship between vaccination and autism. FactCheck.org, which is operated by the Annenberg Public Policy Center, has also challenged claims linking vaccines to autism, explaining that the evidence does not support them.

These misconceptions may have consequences for vaccination decisions. Previous Annenberg research found that people who accept false vaccine claims, including the belief that the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine causes autism, are less likely to recommend MMR vaccination to people who are eligible to receive it.

Only 9% of Americans Know How Deadly Measles Can Be.

The survey uncovered another striking knowledge gap. Most Americans appear uncertain about the risk of death associated with measles in children.

When asked how many children infected with measles are likely to die from the disease, 59% of respondents remarked they did not know. Just 9% selected the correct response, "about 1 in 1,000," which most closely matches the CDC’s estimate that 1 to 3 of every 1,000 infected children die from respiratory or neurological complications.

Nearly one-quarter of respondents (23%) underestimated the death rate, while another 9% selected a higher rate.

In a recent development, knowledge about measles vaccination was also limited. Almost half of Americans (49%) said they were unsure how many doses children need for full protection. Only about one-third (34%) correctly identified the recommended two-dose schedule.

The CDC advises giving children their first MMR vaccine dose between 12 and 15 months of age, followed by a second dose between ages 4 and 6. According to CDC data, a single dose provides 93% protection against measles, while receiving both doses increases effectiveness to 97%.

Public Confidence in Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Remains Low.

In a recent development, the survey also examined Americans' trust in U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The findings indicate that public confidence in his health-related communications has changed little since earlier surveys conducted in 2025 and 2026.

It has been revealed that in November 2026, about six in 10 respondents (61%) noted they were not confident that Kennedy was providing trustworthy information about public health. The remaining four in 10 (39%) expressed confidence in the information he provides.

These results are consistent with seven earlier national probability surveys conducted over two years (February 2025 to August 2026). During that period, 60% to 63% of respondents reported lacking confidence in Kennedy, while 37% to 39% expressed confidence.

Kathleen Hall Jamieson, director of the Annenberg Public Policy Center's Science of Science Communication Institute and its ASAPH and ASK surveys, remarked the loss of measles elimination status demonstrates the consequences of declining vaccination coverage.

"The announcement that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status confirms what we already knew," stated Kathleen Hall Jamieson. "Those who refused the MMR vaccine for themselves or their children and those who misled them into doing so have produced the tragic effects that science predicted would occur when community immunity dropped below the threshold needed to protect those who are not able to be vaccinated or refused to be.".

How the National Measles Survey Was Conducted.

The findings draw on two types of Annenberg Science and Public Health (ASAPH) surveys.

The November 2026 results come from a nationally representative survey of 1,028 U.S. adults conducted for APPC by SSRS, an independent market research organization. Participants were selected from the manufacturer's probability-based online opinion panel, and responses were collected Nov. 6-8, 2026. The survey has a margin of sampling error (MOE) of ± 3.5 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.

Sources indicate that the other findings come from APPC's ongoing ASAPH panel surveys, which are also administered by SSRS. Participants were originally recruited through probability sampling from the SSRS Opinion Panel, and their responses are weighted to reflect the U.S. adult population. This research panel operates separately from the SSRS Omnibus survey and has completed more than 30 survey waves since April 2021.

Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number, so totals may not always equal 100%.

Additional results are available in the survey topline, which includes data from both the November 2026 omnibus survey and the ongoing ASAPH panel surveys. A separate methodology statement provides further details about the latest survey.

Since April 2021, the Annenberg Public Policy Center has used its Annenberg Science and Public Health (ASAPH) research program and separate national samples to monitor Americans' knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to vaccines, Covid-19, influenza, RSV, and other important health issues.

It has been revealed that the APPC health survey team includes Ken Winneg, managing director of survey research; Laura A. Gibson, research analyst; and Patrick E. Jamieson, director of the Annenberg Health and Risk Communication Institute.

Sources indicate that materials provided by Annenberg Public Policy Center of the University of Pennsylvania. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • These days, I’m particularly interested in cars of the past.
  • The Patent Motorwagen gets credit for being first because Carl Benz designed it to be a car from the get-go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

These days, I’m particularly interested in cars of the past. By that I mean the distant past. Such is the case for the 1886 Benz Patent Motorwagen I drove during Monterey Car Week. Now when someone asks, “What’s the oldest car you’ve ever driven?” I have an unassailable answer. That is, unless you’ve driven Cugnot’s steam car. You did? No way. Was it cool?

The Patent Motorwagen gets credit for being first because Carl Benz designed it to be a car from the get-go. He didn’t simply take a horse-drawn carriage, add an engine and drivetrain, subtract the horse and reins, carry the oats.

In a recent development, I love primordial stuff because things we take for granted today had not yet been figured out. There were lots of guesses—some right, others not. Driving a vehicle that old is disorienting, challenging, and sometimes dangerous. Maybe something will explode. Maybe you’ll fall out. Boring hadn’t been engineered into the experience yet.

See all results for used cars for sale near 70802.

Recent findings suggest that the Patent Motorwagen gives big perambulator vibes, and baby, I am here for it. It has only three wheels, to keep it simple and light. Carriages turned their entire axle, since uprights and kingpins at the wheels were still years away. Steering the first car involves grabbing what appears to be the wood handle of an awl—the automotive steering wheel hadn’t been invented yet either. Also not in existence in 1886: carburetor jets, engine radiators, radios, tetanus shots.

Another hitherto unimagined concept: hiding the crankshaft and flywheel behind casings. The crank, connecting rod, cam gear, and drive belt all sit out in the open. Some of those parts have to be greased up before your drive. For others, oil is metered out onto the cylinder and the intake valve by drip lubricators before it runs over less critical parts and leaves behind a greasy trail on the road.

To start the Benz, switch on the ignition that sends energy to the roughly eight-inch-long spark plug, then grab the horizontal flywheel. Give that a Wheel of Fortune–worthy spin and wait. The air-hexane fuel mixture is adjustable, so you can richen it to help the car start (it originally ran on naphtha, which was available at apothecaries in 1886, right next to the laudanum). There’s no throttle, so the 1.0-liter doesn’t stray far from its 400-rpm operating speed. A 4.8-quart copper vessel perched over the engine holds the water that cools the cylinder. After about an hour of operation, the water boils over, and you stop and take a calf’s-head-stew break to let things cool.

To accelerate, push the long lever on the left side of the leather-trimmed park bench to engage the engine-driven leather strap to the axle. Feel the 0.88 horsepower. To stop, pull that lever back to actuate a shoe that drags on the axle. Not to sound like an 1886 infomercial, but driving the Patent Motorwagen is so easy, a toddler could do it. It’ll hit a claimed 13 mph, and it was the most amazing 13 mph I’ve ever experienced. There’s no way I’m going to be this fun when I’m 140 years old.

See all results for used cars for sale near 70802.

Senior features editor Elana Scherr shares my fondness for the supercentenarian set. She owns a 1915 Dodge, making her the perfect person to organize a U.S. equivalent of Britain’s London-to-Brighton race for early cars. I rode along and got to exceed a 45-mph speed limit in a 116-year-old Pullman, ancient proof that speed limits are set too low. Not to worry, I was running Waze. Scherr’s account begins on page 64.

According to recent reports, if you aren’t in the mood to go antiquing, there’s a 795-hp Mustang on page 34, a nearly 1000-hp Audi super car on page 58, and the newly introduced Corvette Grand Sport on page 72. Encompassing both new and old, this is a great glitch.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, leonida was named after the fictional state in which GTA 6 takes place, and it was one of several attempts to get the console version running on a computer.
  • The developers had asked users to supply their own game files, but Take-Two argues that the project was designed specifically to make use of the leaked build.
  • Industry observers note that gitHub states it acted on the entire network of 3,007 repositories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, leonida was named after the fictional state in which GTA 6 takes place, and it was one of several attempts to get the console version running on a computer. Unlike some of the fan-made PC ports we've seen for older console games, though, this one was being developed using a build of a game that had only just come out.

The developers had asked users to supply their own game files, but Take-Two argues that the project was designed specifically to make use of the leaked build. The manufacturer requested that GitHub take down Leonida and its forks, arguing that the alleged infringement couldn't be addressed without disabling the repositories altogether.

Industry observers note that gitHub states it acted on the entire network of 3,007 repositories. That number includes forks, which are essentially copies of a repository that other GitHub people can work on independently. That doesn't mean there were 3,007 different GTA 6 PC ports in development, though.

An Xbox Series build of GTA 6 was leaked on November 20, with the Leonida repository appearing a day later.

It has been revealed that according to PC Gamer, the team appeared to have reached the game's splash screen during a livestream before it crashed. The project's lead developer, NotRexed, subsequently announced their departure, citing the loss of the Discord server as well as the pressure of managing the community alongside school and sports.

It has been revealed that take-Two's takedown hasn't put an end to Leonida, either. According to the same report, others have already tried to pick up where the original developer left off.

It's a familiar situation for those of us who primarily play on PC. GTA 4 came to PC several months after its console debut, while we had to wait more than a year and a half after GTA 5's original launch for its PC version. Even Red Dead Redemption 2 took roughly a year to make its way over.

Sources indicate that the difference this time is that a report has suggested GTA 6 could arrive on PC in the first quarter of 2027. If that turns out to be true, the wait would be much shorter than it was for Rockstar's last two major releases. There hasn't been an official announcement confirming that release window, however.

In a recent development, getting GTA 6 to boot on a PC and getting it to run well enough to play through the entire game are two very different things. Just look at how badly Rockstar handled GTA 4's PC port. Even hardware that far exceeded the game's original system requirements struggled to run it smoothly, and Rockstar never bothered to properly fix it.

Recent findings suggest that modders have spent years ironing out its performance problems and bugs, and while that's still an ongoing process, I'd argue 2026 has been the best year yet to play GTA 4 on PC. Even if one of these unofficial efforts eventually makes it past the splash screen, there's no telling how well the game will run on a typical gaming PC or whether it'll have major bugs throughout the story.

Hopefully, Rockstar won't keep us in the dark for too long regarding the official PC version. Even an approximate release window would be welcome at this point, especially for anyone holding off on buying a console just to play GTA 6.

It has been revealed that welcome to Car and Driver’s Testing Hub, where we zoom in on the test numbers. We’ve been pushing vehicles to their limits since 1956 to provide objective data to bolster our subjective impressions (you can see how we test here).

The debut of the 2026 Lexus ES brought a full overhaul to the luxury sedan, which included a revamped hybrid variant. The newly introduced generation comes with fresh styling, a longer wheelbase, and an updated powertrain. In our testing, a 2026 ES350h was considerably quicker than a 2023 Lexus ES300h F Sport Handling, which was the last ES hybrid we tested.

See all results for fresh 2026 Lexus ES for sale near 92804.

According to recent reports, in our recent test of the ES350h, the updated sedan sprinted to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, while the 2023 car more or less jogged its way to the 60-mph mark in 7.9 seconds. That’s a huge improvement, and one that took us by surprise, given that the new car doesn’t look drastically more powerful than the old one on paper. That’s to say nothing of the additional 352 pounds of weight in the new car either.

So, where did all the extra quickness come from? Well, we can think of several places. For starters, the 2026 ES hybrid is more powerful, even if the numbers don’t jump off the page. The powertrain, which features a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, now churns out 244 horsepower, up from 215 in the 2023 ES. Along with a more powerful engine, the updated hybrid system uses a larger and more powerful electric drive motor than the previous generation. Lexus also now offers the gas-electric ES with all-wheel drive for the first time, and that’s the version we tested, with the additional traction helping offset the newly introduced car’s weight gain.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced generation also moved from a 3.39:1 axle ratio to a 3.44:1 axle ratio, a change that increases low-end torque at the wheels and makes the newer car somewhat punchier off the line. Lastly, the 2026 car gets a larger hybrid battery that can provide more horsepower than the smaller unit in the previous ES.

None of the changes are individually earth-shattering—especially with the extra 352 pounds of weight—but add them together, and the ES hybrid is a much quicker car than before.

The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on.

All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they confirmed a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".

Recent findings suggest that the lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation". In a press release, they say they've filed suit on behalf of anybody who bought Intel stock from July 23rd to October 29th this year.

The suit claims that Intel neglected to tell investors that falling PC and component sales were having a "materially greater negative impact" on their third financial quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Groupresults than Intel had previously stated – to the tune of "hundreds of millions of dollars" in revenue shrinkage, compared to the previous quarter, with the situation still expected to "worsen".

They also accuse the firm of keeping schtum about the aforesaid "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", together with the fact that "any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup described above.".

Sources indicate that finally, they say Intel bosses have failed to disclose that they're struggling to procure an adequate supply of substrates – that is, materials used to create the base layer of chips, circuit boards and similar components. As such, the lawyers claim, Intel couldn't "ramp up production to meet data center CPU demand even if the Company chose to divert production resources because of a slowdown in PC-related sales.".

According to recent reports, once the Godzilla of personal computing, Intel haven't been having a brilliant few years. Back in 2024, they recorded a multi-billion dollar quarterly loss, pushing then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to resign. As regards sales of gaming PCs, they've fallen behind AMD, though they've reportedly taken some ground back recently as regards desktop CPUs. As regards graphics cards, they have long been dwarfed by Nvidia.

Breaking: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why does being awake for too long make us increasingly desperate for sleep?
  • According to recent reports, the longer we go without sleep, the more difficult it becomes to stay awake.
  • Industry observers note that researchers led by Professor Alex Schier at the Biozentrum, University of Basel, have now identified brain cells that help regulate this process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why does being awake for too long make us increasingly desperate for sleep? Scientists at the University of Basel in Switzerland have identified two groups of brain cells in mice that become more active the longer the animals remain awake. These neurons play a critical role in creating the pressure to sleep, offering newly introduced clues about how the brain regulates our need for rest.

According to recent reports, the longer we go without sleep, the more difficult it becomes to stay awake. This buildup of sleep pressure, often called sleep drive, helps ensure that extended periods of wakefulness are followed by longer and deeper sleep. Although sleep is essential for survival, exactly how the brain measures time spent awake and converts that information into an increasing need for sleep has remained a mystery.

Industry observers note that researchers led by Professor Alex Schier at the Biozentrum, University of Basel, have now identified brain cells that help regulate this process. The work was conducted in collaboration with scientists from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Auburn University.

Sources indicate that "We have identified neuronal populations that monitor prolonged wakefulness and actively promote sleep," indicates Alex Schier. "This is an vital missing piece of the puzzle in understanding why we become sleepy.".

Scientists Identify Brain Cells That Drive Sleep Pressure.

To investigate how sleep pressure develops, the team studied patterns of brain activity in mice under three different conditions: normal cycles of sleeping and waking, extended sleep deprivation, and recovery sleep. By comparing these patterns, they identified brain regions whose activity changed according to how long the animals had been awake.

Industry observers note that within one of these regions, the brainstem, researchers pinpointed two groups of neurons involved in controlling sleep drive. Known as GABAergic and serotonergic neurons, both groups became progressively more active as the mice remained awake. Their activity then decreased once the animals fell asleep.

The next question was whether these neurons simply tracked how long the mice had been awake or actually helped create the growing need for sleep.

In a recent development, experiments revealed that the neurons were directly involved in driving sleep. When researchers artificially activated both groups, the mice slept longer and more deeply, showing the same type of recovery sleep normally seen after extended wakefulness. When the neurons were inhibited, however, the animals slept substantially less and were able to remain awake and alert.

Sources indicate that "These neurons do not simply signal that an animal has been awake," states Schier. "Our experiments show that they are crucial to promote sleep, and that they may be key components of the neural circuitry that generates sleep drive.".

The results provide particularly strong evidence that certain neurons activated during wakefulness do more than register lost sleep. They actively help generate the pressure that eventually pushes the brain toward sleep.

Mice Sleep 70% Less When Key Neurons Are Inhibited.

In a recent development, further experiments produced an especially surprising result. When scientists suppressed both groups of neurons for an extended period, the mice slept approximately 70% less than normal.

Even more unexpectedly, most of these animals did not display some of the serious behavioral problems typically associated with prolonged sleep deprivation. Despite getting dramatically less sleep, many avoided impairments that researchers would ordinarily expect.

These findings suggest that the identified neurons influence not only the amount of time animals spend sleeping, but also how strongly the pressure to sleep increases during wakefulness.

Rather than simply responding to exhaustion, the brain appears to use specific neural circuits to actively regulate the growing need for rest.

A New Direction for Sleep Research.

It has been revealed that understanding these circuits could open important new avenues for studying sleep and its effects on the body. Researchers now hope to determine how the identified neurons communicate with other brain regions and what molecular processes allow them to generate sleep pressure.

Industry observers note that "Future studies could reveal how these neurons interact with the rest of the brain, and how sleep drive is generated at the molecular level," says Dr. William Joo, first author of the study. "Our ability to stably transform sleep behavior also allows us to explore adaptations to long-term sleep loss - this may eventually reveal ways to confer resilience to sleep deprivation and other physiological challenges.".

The findings establish that GABAergic and serotonergic neurons in the brainstem become increasingly active during prolonged wakefulness and play an essential role in promoting sleep.

Determining exactly how the brain makes sleep increasingly difficult to resist remains a major objective of sleep research. Beyond improving scientists' understanding of sleep disorders, this discovery could help explain how the nervous system adapts to extended wakefulness and other physical challenges.

Ultimately, a clearer understanding of the brain circuits responsible for sleep pressure could inspire new treatments and potentially reveal ways to improve resilience to sleep deprivation.

America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, america's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up.
  • It has been revealed that in a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission.
  • America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, america's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up. More electric vehicles, increased electricity use in heavy industry, and the explosive growth of data centers are driving demand higher, putting additional pressure on an infrastructure system that is already falling behind.

It has been revealed that in a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission. The problem could have major consequences for electricity prices, grid reliability, and the nation's economic future.

America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.

A major concern is the extremely slow pace of transmission construction. Over the past five years, the continental United States has added an average of only about 500 miles of high-voltage transmission lines annually. Research suggests the country needs approximately 5,000 miles each year to triple the size of its interregional transmission network by 2050 and accommodate future electricity demand.

Recent findings suggest that that means the U.S. is building newly introduced high-voltage transmission lines at just one-tenth of the estimated pace needed.

It has been revealed that high-voltage transmission lines serve as the highways of the electricity system, carrying large amounts of power over long distances from generating facilities to communities and businesses. Connecting regional grids allows electricity to flow more easily between areas, helping balance supply and demand when local power production falls short.

Studies have shown that larger, better-connected electricity networks can reduce costs for consumers while also lowering the risk of catastrophic blackouts. When one region experiences a power shortage, electricity from another region can help keep the lights on.

Despite these advantages, expanding the nation's transmission infrastructure has proved extraordinarily difficult.

The Biggest Obstacle Isn't Technology.

In a recent development, according to the researchers (Madeline Yozwiak, David G. Victor, and M. Granger Morgan), the main barriers to modernizing America's power grid are political and regulatory rather than technological.

In a recent development, responsibility for approving major transmission projects is divided among federal agencies, state governments, local authorities, and private companies. Each has its own priorities and interests, creating numerous opportunities for proposed power lines to be delayed or blocked.

Existing electric utilities can also have financial reasons to resist stronger connections between regions. Greater competition from electricity suppliers elsewhere could weaken their influence over local markets, reducing the incentive to support projects that would benefit the broader electricity system.

As a result, even transmission projects that could lower costs and improve reliability across the country can struggle to gain approval.

Three Ways to Fix America's Power Grid Crisis.

To address the growing shortfall, the researchers recommend a three-part strategy combining stronger government action, modern transmission technologies, international cooperation, and regulatory reform.

It has been revealed that 1. Make better use of existing federal powers and advanced technologies.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the Department of Energy (DOE) already have legal authorities that could help move crucial transmission projects forward. The researchers argue that these agencies should use those powers more effectively, including identifying transmission corridors of national importance and addressing disputes that prevent projects from receiving state-level approval.

Sources indicate that technological improvements could also dramatically increase the amount of electricity the grid can carry. One approach, known as reconductoring, involves replacing existing power line conductors with more advanced materials capable of transmitting more electricity without necessarily requiring entirely newly introduced routes.

Recent findings suggest that other advances, including newer High-Voltage Direct Current (VSC-HVDC) systems, offer additional ways to move large amounts of electricity efficiently. The researchers suggest that modern transmission technologies could double or even triple capacity.

Underground high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables offer another promising option. These systems can carry substantial amounts of electricity over long distances and could potentially be installed along existing highways and railroad corridors. Using these established routes could help avoid some of the land-use disputes and approval challenges that often delay conventional transmission projects.

2. Learn from countries that have already overcome similar obstacles.

The United States trails several international counterparts in building long-distance HVDC infrastructure and coordinating electricity transmission across regional and national boundaries.

Other countries have demonstrated that large transmission projects can move forward despite complicated political approval processes. Some have also successfully deployed underground HVDC systems on a large scale.

According to recent reports, rather than developing every solution independently, the researchers suggest that the U.S. should study these international experiences and adapt approaches that have already proved successful.

One proposal is to establish an international forum involving electricity regulators and other experts, potentially led by organizations such as the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC). Such a forum could help American policymakers identify effective regulatory practices, planning strategies, and technologies used elsewhere.

According to recent reports, 3. Create a national commission to break the political deadlock.

The researchers also recommend establishing a Presidential-Congressional Transmission Commission to address the political and regulatory conflicts that have slowed grid expansion for decades.

Modeled on previous successful bipartisan commissions, the proposed group would bring together key stakeholders to negotiate difficult decisions and develop a coordinated plan for reform.

Its responsibilities would include recommending changes to state and federal laws, examining whether FERC should receive broader authority over the locations of upcoming transmission projects, and developing financial incentives for companies that lead new construction.

The commission could also recommend financial rewards for communities that host transmission infrastructure, helping ensure that local residents share in the benefits of projects that serve larger regions.

Why America's Power Grid Crisis Could Get Worse.

The researchers emphasize that the underlying challenge is not a lack of engineering solutions. Instead, the country's divided decision-making system allows individual stakeholders to obstruct projects that could deliver substantial nationwide benefits.

Industry observers note that "The fundamental challenge isn't technical, it's jurisdictional. Authority is divided among federal, state, and private entities, each with distinct priorities. When every stakeholder possesses the power to say no, even high-value projects that benefit the entire nation struggle to move forward," the authors warn.

Their assessment suggests that simply continuing with the existing system of overlapping regulations and fragmented authority will not be enough to meet America's growing electricity needs.

Without meaningful changes to how transmission projects are planned, approved, and built, the United States risks a prolonged infrastructure shortfall. The researchers warn that failing to resolve these problems could weaken electricity reliability and inflict lasting damage on the national economy, even as demand for power continues to climb.

Each new GTA moves the series closer and closer to the original Mafia, the open-world game that bettered Rockstar

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer.
  • Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.
  • Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer. Naturally, over on PC we're still waiting for a port to be announced, let alone a release date to circle in our calendars. But, as happens whenever a newly introduced GTA is on the horizon, I think about Mafia: City of Lost Heaven.

Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.

Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.

The influences on developers Illusion Softworks are obviously cinematic, with whole sequences ripped from The Godfather films and Goodfellas (and I'd argue there's a sprinkling of Once Upon A Time In America for good measure). A habit they share with Rockstar, who also pull liberally from crime films that share the settings of their games. But Illusion Softworks are also clearly interested in capturing the history of the Prohibition era, too. The story begins in the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed, running through until the late 30s, and you see that time pass in the city around you. Buildings that are under construction at the start of the game are completed by its end, a used car lot in Chinatown sits empty for most of the game until business picks up with the economy, but most enjoyable of all is that the cars driving the streets change. At first the roads are filled with Ford Model-T-inspired vehicles that basically look like horse carriages with engines, but by the end of the game they've all become much sleeker creatures that have left their early carriage influences behind.

It has been revealed that the city Illusion Softworks built also has a dedication to verisimilitude that we see Rockstar adopting in their later games. As you drive Lost Heaven's streets, you must pay attention to speed limits and red lights, as speeding and running traffic lights will both earn you a fine if a policeman spots you. For fans of public transport, there are streetcars and overhead trams you can ride to navigate the city, too. Two other touches I love: when you reload your gun, you dump the whole clip instead of returning the unfired bullets to a magic ammo reservoir, and vehicles can run out of fuel if you drive them too far.

Much had been made of all the simulations running under the surface of Grand Theft Auto 6, such as fully realised cloud formation, a smell reaction system, and… fuel tanks that can run empty. No doubt they're significantly more impressive than what's on show in Mafia, and this isn't about putting the two games against each other (even if one of them was likely made for less than the other studio spent on coffee runs across its eight-year development). Nor is it about saying history recognised the wrong game: Grand Theft Auto 3 was a huge step forward in open-world gaming and Mafia was recognised and celebrated in its time. It's about something else.

Back in 2002, Illusion Softworks offered a different kind of open-world crime game. One that was more mature despite having a lower age rating. Grand Theft Auto was undoubtedly more influential, sparking imitators that mostly opted to follow its tone and sensibilities – Saints Row began in a similar place to GTA 3 and as the series continued leaned further into the silliness and parody, for instance. But while for many years Mafia stood as a sign to an open world path that could have been taken, the longer Grand Theft Auto series has gone on, the more Rockstar have found their way toward the example set by Illusion Softworks. The games are still aiming for bombastic comedy at times, but they're also interested in the likes of newly-arrived-in-America Niko Belic, or Michael de Santa, a retired criminal haunted by his past. They're much richer protagonists than Claude, the silent character you play in GTA 3.

According to recent reports, the Mafia series has continued, marked by ideas that remain as interesting as what was on show in the original. In Mafia 3, you play Lincoln Clay, a black soldier returned from the war in Vietnam and brought into the family. Set in a take on Fresh Orleans, Louisiana, during the civil rights movement, you face overt racism. Linger too long in white, wealthy neighbourhoods and the residents will call on the police to move you along. And the Definitive Edition remake of the first game, released in 2020, is a rare example of a game that both captures the spirit of the original and justifies its existence by expanding and bettering the story. Though I don't think any of its sequels have been as innovative, nor as forward thinking, as the first game.

Industry observers note that I don't want to come across as Rockstar-bashing. The studio have continued to push the open-world genre forward with every release and I want to see what other developers lift from GTA 6 for their own games. Company of Heroes 3: Operation Torch Review

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that company of Heroes 3 has come a long way since its 2023 release, slowly making its way to the real-time strategy hall of fame after a rather rough start.
  • Industry observers note that update 3.0 helped bring the game to its full potential, but mechanical polish only goes so far.
  • The dynamic campaign remains the highlight of Organization of Heroes 3, but thanks to Operation Torch, the game finally has a scripted, story campaign that’s worth the trouble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that company of Heroes 3 has come a long way since its 2023 release, slowly making its way to the real-time strategy hall of fame after a rather rough start. And yet, until now, something was missing.

Industry observers note that update 3.0 helped bring the game to its full potential, but mechanical polish only goes so far. Until recently, Tech giant of Heroes 3 was a brilliant strategy game with strong mechanics that lend themselves well to single-player, but this was offset by a lack of quality content you could go through solo.

The dynamic campaign remains the highlight of Organization of Heroes 3, but thanks to Operation Torch, the game finally has a scripted, story campaign that’s worth the trouble.

Operation Torch is the first single-player campaign DLC for Company of Heroes 3. It was preceded by the unorthodox yet highly entertaining Final Stand tower defence DLC, but surviving wave after wave of German tanks is no substitute for a touching story.

According to recent reports, in that sense, the choice to depict Operation Torch is a poetic one. While American forces were being put through wringer in Pacific islands, the US had yet to launch any major land operations against the Germans and Italians.

The North Africa landings sent a green Army against veteran enemies. The Americans turned out to be quite adept at learning on the job, but the lessons there were written in blood. As a DLC, Operation Torch is similar.

Company of Heroes 3 emerges victorious once you see it through, but that success comes on the back of some blunders and failures that I hope are not repeated if or when Relic Entertainment decides another story-driven DLC is due.

The DLC focuses on three American soldiers from the US Army’s 34th Infantry Division, all the way from the landings in Algeria to the crushing of Axis resistance in Tunisia.

As far as individual story beats go, Operation Torch is adequate. Becker, Russo and Flanagan are likeable and quite distinct, and their commentary enhances the missions for the most part. There are some occasional immersion-breaking bits that strike out as silly, just about all of them relating to ‘tutorial’ speech.

For example, in a rather late mission in the campaign, Becker instructs us to defend fuel points because “we need the fuel to build tanks.” Well yes, Colonel, in game we do, but I’m operating under the assumption that these tanks were manufactured in a plant somewhere in Detroit rather than spontaneously spawned through good vibes and virtual resources somewhere in Tunisia.

This is nowhere near as egregious as in the much-maligned Rommel campaign that comes with the base game, but it would have been nice to have the option to disable tutorial-style objectives and commentary for people who are familiar with the game or who are going for a second playthrough.

I need to emphasize repeat playthroughs here because, although Operation Torch is a linear, story-based DLC, it incorporates lessons from other Firm of Heroes 3 releases that make it more replayable than other campaigns in a similar vein.

According to recent reports, most missions are fairly open-ended in terms of how you can approach them. This is complemented by a decent degree of customization after each mission depending on how you accomplish both primary and secondary objectives. The Italy campaign had similar choices, but the Operation Torch system is closer to that of the Final Stand DLC.

Recent findings suggest that the effects of the upgrades you pick are rather tangible. For example, early on, I managed to unlock M3 assault halftracks as a command call-in. Despite being rather underwhelming in their basic battle taxi configuration, these can be converted into game-changers.

The Americans turned out to be quite adept at learning on the job, but the lessons there were written in blood.

Many of my missions were saved because I was able to bring in an M3 converted into 75mm gun carriers that provided quick, on-call artillery support to break down defenses. When dug in myself, the M16 variant with the .50 quad-mounts made mince out of Axis infantry, allowing outnumbered defenders to hold out. All of this could have gone differently had I chosen another upgrade perk, which would have had its own advantages.

Final Stand’s influence is particularly felt in those defensive scenarios, where its wave mechanics reach their zenith.

Base game mechanics sometimes make these last stands slightly less dramatic than they could be at first, primarily because, as in real life, liberal application of engineering obstacles and overlapping fields of fire make incoming waves trivial. That false sense of safety comes apart spectacularly once heavier armor rolls in and you learn that Bazookas can’t dent it.

According to recent reports, relic managed to craft missions that reward sound tactics. Generally speaking, if it works in real life, it will work here. There is one exception that deserves its own section, and that’s the abysmal commando raid mission.

When the Operation Torch announcement came about late last month, the commando gameplay was by far the most exciting part. I’ve been counting the days until SAS: Rogue Heroes comes back for its third season, and I was hoping the commando levels would be a good way to make the wait easier. I was sorely mistaken, I’m afraid.

The level where you plant explosive charges is an affront to modern game design, primarily because it is just… Pac-Man. With guns.

You play one lonely commando, and your job is to slip by German patrols to plant demolition charges on 88mm guns. Every time you die (which, in my experience, is a lot), you respawn on the last checkpoint. Besides snipers, taking out any enemy does virtually nothing as they respawn almost immediately as well.

The result is a level that’s both archaic and devoid of meaning. There’s no way to fail the mission, as you just keep sending more and more single commandos into the breech, the Germans reciprocate, and you’re sitting there playing Pac-Man timing patrol movement patterns for a dry 30 minutes.

The mission is a one off, much like the American debacle in the Kasserine Pass in February 1943, but it leaves a mark on what’s otherwise a well-built campaign with strong design and balancing.

Playing Operation Torch and the Italy campaign back-to-back has been great because you get to see how far Allied land operations in the Mediterranean Theater of Operations have come from the shaky landings in Algeria to the assault on Monte Cassino that opened the road to Rome.

It’s nice to see an oft-forgotten part of World War 2 history given the attention it deserves. The British and German versions of the fight for North Africa have been told a million times over, but with a few exceptions (most notably Call of Duty 2: Big Red One), the American African campaign is constantly overshadowed by later exploits in Europe and the Pacific.

Operation Torch also lays out a blueprint for potential future DLCs that focus on telling stories, rather than just adding upcoming units to the same old multiplayer slog. The combined force of this DLC with patch 3.0 released earlier this month puts Tech giant of Heroes 3 in the spot it was always meant to occupy since its launch.

Relic made a bold choice in depicting Operation Torch to this degree, and it paid off in spades. Tech giant of Heroes 3 mechanics come alive in a fight that doesn’t get the attention it deserves, in spite of occasional hiccups. The first narrative-driven DLC for the game indicates that there’s plenty of untapped potential in it, and it’s left me hoping more of them will come.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mega Man: Dual Override’s 2025 reveal brought back the classic boss design contest, asking fans to create and submit their own robot masters, with Capcom choosing one to include in the game. After thousands of submissions, we have our winner; meet Cleanser Man.

As his name suggests, Cleanser Man is a cleaning robot who attacks (and tidies) using a long, multi-cleaning hose arm. Capcom has provided the following character summary:.

Cleanser Man is a cleaning robot with an obsession for pristine beauty. Fueled by an extremely sensitive dirt sensor, Cleaner Man’s ideal world is one without a speck of dust. However, his devotion to cleanliness has a cost. His aggressive scrubbing causes great damage to global landmarks and historic works of art. This fixation has caused the public to view him as more of a threat than a helping hand. Furious and feeling misunderstood, Cleanser Man seizes control of trash processing facility and uses it to pollute the environment with hopes of forcing the world to appreciate the importance of cleanliness.

Cleanser Man won out among the six finalists, a few of which were also cleaning-themed bosses. “In the end, we chose Cleanser Man because of the unique way the concept was brought together and the originality of the color design,” says game director Shinya Ikuta. “While staying true to and respecting the original submission, we adjusted certain details to better fit the world and style of the game.”  Unfortunately, Capcom has not revealed Cleanser Man's creator, but you can see the character in action in the reveal video below.

In addition to Cleanser Man, Mega Man: Dual Override's rogues' gallery includes the following revealed robot masters: Twinkle Girl, Jet Man, Tank Man, and Cook Man. The remaining three bosses have yet to be revealed.

It has been revealed that mega Man: Dual Override releases in 2027 for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC. To learn more about the game, read our extended preview here. You can also check out the game's recently revealed amiibo figures for the Switch versions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the upcoming content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a fresh blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing complications with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

We know that Season 2 is introducing a massive upcoming map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

Industry observers note that the real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the newly introduced season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

Sources indicate that challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

Sources indicate that BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

Audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.
